title.title: The Correspondence of Esther Roberts Hunt Collins

msIdentifier.institution: Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College

projectDesc.p: The correspondence of Quaker minister Esther Roberts Hunt Collins is stored at the Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College. With the generous support of H. David and Joyce E. Hunt, Library staff scanned and transcribed these letters in 2024 and encoded the text in TEI.

div.p: I received thy letter dated 14th 4 month last which was a comfort & satisfaction beyond my expression, to receive a letter of thy hand writing when so widely separated has a feeling: & to here somewhat particular from my dear friends is certainly a great favor.

There has been a desire to hear of your safe arrival home, & some of us would be glad to hear from Thomas Scattergood whether he has returned or not; we have had friends twice over from Virginia since you were here. Their first time to see the situation of our meeting in regard of a request that was made for the dividing our monthly meeting, also the establishing a preparative at Fallowfield—the second time they came by the appointment of the quarter to attend the opening of the monthly meeting which has occasioned some stir & inquiry into the proper manner of transacting business & as we are like a mixed multitude there is a diversity of sentiments, some being accustomed to one way and some another, a meeting of conference was concluded on, which I thought was to a degree of satisfaction
but, when the report was made to the monthly meeting all could not unite there with—the reason I mention this is, to give a little sight, the need there is of a prayer book of advice & discipline, to keep things in decent order, & as there is none here (some heady & strong willed) I can but request thee, to take some pains in getting some parts copied & send us which are most explicit relating to disowning members publicly & on minute with the proper distinction–likewise upon requests to be received amongst friends, & the difference of such as have forfeited their rite, by some misconduct of their’s be—upon their desiring to return— for it is not enough for one to think it should be so, or so, but it is needful for us to be united in the oneness that there be no divisions to weaken us—I suppose the most clear account there is here, is a little part my dear husband brought from brother Samuel which my father had copied of— I wish not to be too tedious to thee, yet, cannot well pass over one little matter that was conferred upon at our little meeting of conference, which was, the way of monthly-meeting, breaking up in order some were for the meeting to be broken up (or concluded) by shakings hands, others with a minute of adjournment which appeared to settle so then, but, when it was proposed to the monthly-meeting for their approbation, it would not bear some knowing ones, thought no meeting less than a yearly meeting had a right to an adjournment—so the matter was debated on, in that wisdom which leads to confusion, or else I was mistaken.
I may give thee some little account of things with us further. Poor William & Jane Silverthorn are at last testified against by friends, & it is said that she is much taken with the Methodists—they are a rich, poor unhappy couple.

William Wilson has buried his son William, a young man about 20 with a short spell of sickness—Henry Smith & Martha his wife have sold their possessions and removed 40 miles farther remote from friends, but, they have faith to think they will come & settle there. I suppose there is a fine outward prospect there— been very still as to alarms about the Indians— many people gone down the river this spring & amongst the rest. Enoch Gause with his family & poor Charles Gause seems at times near selling & going too, they hear such fine accounts from George Harton & his wife who were friends in good esteem that moved down last fall—with unfeigned love to thee thy wife & children, in which mine join. I conclude firmly desiring to be established on that Rock, where the storms & wind will not move–that if we should never see each other more in this world, grant, O Lord, that we may so finish our days that we may be found worthy to meet, were all sorrow shall be wiped away is the breathing desire of my soul.
